projects.title: Starship Booster Cryo Proof Tooling
projects.summary: I redesigned Super Heavy’s cryo-proof tooling to reduce leak paths and make installation repeatable: welded drain elbows, a GOX seal interface, and standard attachment bolts, carried from load calculations into vehicle integration.

points.text: I reviewed the tooling sealing 33 feedlines for leak paths, difficult work access, and assembly errors. That review led to three component redesigns, alongside drain rerouting and mistake-proofing.

I replaced a leak-prone bolted joint stackup with a welded 90° elbow connecting the blankoff to the cryogenic drain tube. The elbow welded directly to the blankoff, leaving one B-nut joint at the flared tube’s AN connection with a copper seal. I chose 304 stainless steel to match the blankoff’s weld material.

points.lead: Size the vehicle-side weld, then control fit-up
points.text: I used the maximum elbow outlet moment and loads from the cryo-proof feedline blow-off cases to size the elbow’s vehicle-side weld to the blankoff using Blodgett’s method. A radial key clocked the outlet; a diameter step located weld height. I toleranced the fit to keep the TIG root gap within 0.5 mm.

I ran Ansys simulations on the revised blankoff geometries, including the new clocking cutouts. I applied pressure to their internal faces based on the maximum feedline blow-off load cases in the cryo-proof test.

points.lead: Improve sealing at a faulty interface
points.text: I designed a Monel bung welded to a stainless blankoff to improve sealing performance at another faulty interface. I controlled the interface geometry to minimize gaseous-oxygen (GOX) impingement risk and sized the dissimilar-metal weld using Blodgett’s method.

The bung protruded through the blankoff and sat against a counterbore in the blankoff to form the inner lip of an upper seal gland. I used the Parker O-Ring Handbook to size the gland for the required O-ring compression.
I evaluated replacing the existing A280 mil-spec bolts with Grade 5 hardware stocked in the factory. I based the sizing on maximum feedline blow-off loads during cryo-proof testing.
From the blow-off force, I calculated the required bolt preload and tightening torque using T = KDF, with K as the torque coefficient, D as bolt diameter, and F as preload.
I checked joint gapping and bolt fatigue under repeated loading. All checks passed, allowing us to replace the specialized bolts with standard Grade 5 hardware.
I released the revised parts and evaluated manufacturing deviations against critical sealing requirements. I then oversaw fabrication of the welded subassemblies.

I oversaw vehicle integration, rerouted drain tubes for work access, and mistake-proofed an asymmetric subassembly. I maintained the 13,000-component CAD assembly across three vehicles at different release states and designed lineside storage to support two vehicles using the tools simultaneously.

projects.note: Design work performed at SpaceX is proprietary. No CAD, drawings, part numbers, or hardware imagery are shown.

projects.decision: Replace bolted stackups with welded interfaces, control weld fit-up with keyed features, and design the seal glands and tube routing around test and integration requirements.
projects.proof: Blodgett weld sizing, internal-pressure Ansys checks, root-gap tolerancing, and empirical seal testing.
projects.takeaway: Interface geometry, weld fit-up, and seal behavior guided the redesign.

projects.title: V3 Starfactory Weld Cell & Integration Tooling
projects.summary: I owned the CONOPS, layout, and tooling design for a V3 Starfactory cell building a ring manifold for oxygen, methane, environmental-control gases, and helium. I carried the work from fixture prototypes through machined tooling, lift planning, and vehicle integration.

points.lead: Plan how the cell would build the manifold
points.text: I defined the concept of operations (CONOPS) and arranged the cell in a semicircle, laying out the slat wall, Siegmund weld tables, and cantilevered racks around the ring-manifold build.

I used the Siegmund table holes to locate the fixtures and kept them clear of the Orbitalum orbital tube welder. The flanged endpoints needed precise position and clocking because they formed critical vehicle passthroughs.
I applied 3-2-1 locating, GD&T, and selected dowel-pin fits to control the endpoints. I also sized tooling seal glands using the Parker O-Ring Handbook.

I quickly 3D-printed fixture components for the first article build, revised the designs from those fit-up lessons, and had the tools machined for subsequent builds. I oversaw the cell’s setup and integration.
I worked with the assembly’s Responsible Engineer to establish rigging points on its brackets, then designed a three-point lift and rigging plan to fly the welded manifold into the vehicle.

points.lead: Size the structure and locate the lugs
points.text: I used bending and deflection calculations to size the 1,100 lb WLL tool. I calculated bracket centers of gravity and placed welded lifting lugs directly above them to prevent tilt. I sized the lug welds so two lugs could carry the entire assembly.

points.lead: Prove the lift and plan installation
points.text: I proof-tested the tool at 2,200 lb, twice its working load limit, and wrote the integration plan for welding the subassembly on the vehicle.
I designed a stand to improve work access during aft flap torque-frame integration. I based its load cases on the maximum forces technicians could apply during assembly.

points.lead: Calculate bending, torsion, and weld loads
points.text: I solved for two-plane bending and maximum torsion, then used those loads to size the integration stand and its welds.
I took precise measurements of existing assemblies and created as-built CAD models of the off-nominal conditions.
I used those models to design five flight-part retrofits for manufacture and installation on the existing assemblies.
I designed additional tools, including 3D-printed and Protolabs parts, to support cell integration and improve the production process.

projects.headline: V3 Starfactory Weld Cell & Integration Tooling
projects.challenge: Control manifold flange fit-up and improve access and handling during Starship assembly.
projects.decision: Use self-clocking weld fixtures, load-sized handling tools, and measured as-built CAD for flight-part retrofits.
projects.proof: GD&T-controlled flange fixtures, a 2,200 lb lift proof test, and five flight-part retrofits.
projects.takeaway: Locate the hardware accurately, then design around how it will be assembled.

projects.title: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.summary: I designed the rotor and mount for reliable braking within the drivetrain package, combining material tradeoffs, thermal analysis, structural FEA, and temperature testing.

points.text: I compared cast iron and 4140 steel and selected steel for its endurance-limit advantage. Titanium buttons limited heat transfer into the 7075 aluminum mount, which I packaged at the differential bolts.

points.lead: Thickness: bound and refine the heat load
points.text: For the 500°C requirement, I first sized thickness assuming maximum braking energy became heat with no heat escaping. I refined that conservative estimate with transient conduction, forced convection, and radiation analysis.

points.lead: Geometry: manage debris and check stress
points.text: I added curved face slots for debris removal, de-gassing, and water clearance, accepting additional pad wear. In Ansys, I supported the pad contact regions and applied braking moment through the mount connections to check stress.
The rotors were manufactured through outsourced three-axis CNC machining. I used temperature crayons to assess their operating temperatures.

projects.headline: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.challenge: Coordinate the rotor packaging with the powertrain team and design for long-term reliability, with a 500°C temperature requirement and a safety margin.
projects.decision: Compare cast iron with 4140 steel, use titanium buttons to limit heat flow into an aluminum mount, and refine rotor thickness through transient thermal analysis.
projects.proof: Checked the rotor in Ansys with supports at the pad contact regions and braking moment applied through the mount bolt locations. Used temperature crayons to assess operating temperatures and outsourced manufacturing to a three-axis CNC supplier.
projects.takeaway: Long-term reliability guided the material choices, thermal sizing, and structural checks.

caliperSelection.rationale: Sponsorship availability was the deciding factor. The Brembo had the largest listed pad area, tied the ISR for the largest listed piston area, and weighed less than the ISR. The AP Racing option was lighter and the Wilwood was less expensive; the comparison did not identify a clear winner across all criteria.

projects.title: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.summary: I designed a rear hub and bearing assembly that brought the drivetrain, wheel, and electronics interfaces together in a lightweight, manufacturable package.

points.text: I defined the hub around the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and the electronics team’s Hall sensors. I screened bearings in SKF SimPro Quick for load capacity, fatigue life, and power loss within an 80–85 mm bore and 110–120 mm outer-diameter envelope; the selection set hub thickness and packaging.
I compared titanium, 6061, and 7075 aluminum and selected 7075-T6. Its higher yield strength than 6061 supported the hub’s structural requirements.

I applied wheel loads from the team’s truss solver to the wheel flange, modeled the tensile load from the center-lock nut, and included bearing forces and drivetrain torque at the tripod interface. I sized hub-nut engagement using bolt tensile and nut thread-shear areas.
I built the geometry around the interfaces and selected bearing, removed excess material through pocketing, and checked the revised hub in Ansys.
Rotational features were turned first; CNC milling then produced the tripod cutout, pin and button holes, and flange pockets.

projects.headline: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.challenge: Define a rear hub assembly around the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and the electronics team’s Hall effect sensors, while meeting structural and manufacturing requirements.
projects.decision: Use the system interfaces and bearing selection to establish the hub geometry and thickness, compare titanium with 6061 and 7075 aluminum, then size the threaded hub nut connection and optimize pocketing with FEA.
projects.proof: Checked cornering and braking loads, bearing performance in SKF SimPro Quick, and hub behavior in Ansys. Manufacturing included lathe operations on several features and tooling the part for a three-axis CNC mill.
projects.takeaway: The drivetrain and electronics interfaces set the requirements. Bearing selection, structural analysis, and machining constraints then shaped the hub.
projects.discipline: System integration / Bearing selection / Mechanical design

bearingSelection.method: Build the assembly in SKF SimPro Quick and sweep the candidate bearings. Work with Powertrain to set the allowable inner diameter.
bearingSelection.validation: Selected the SKF 71817 ACDGB/VQ253 angular-contact bearing after reviewing fatigue life, load capacity, and power loss across wheel speeds.

projects.title: Carbon Pushrod & Swept Control Arms
projects.summary: I developed and fabricated a lighter suspension assembly, pairing carbon-fiber pushrods with steel control arms and checking both the bonded joints and on-car clearance.

points.lead: Materials: reduce mass within shop capability
points.text: I kept steel control arms because the team had greater confidence in that manufacturing process, and switched the pushrods to carbon fiber to reduce mass. Apex-mounted gussets replaced a heavy mounting plate.

I tested the carbon-fiber pushrods in tension and compression on an Instron. For fabrication, I cut the tubes to length and turned aluminum end plugs, controlling the bonding-surface diameter to within half a thousandth of an inch.

points.lead: Fabrication: carry the geometry into hardware
points.text: I cut steel tubing, turned and milled end plugs, bored and reamed bearing seats in laser-cut plates, and welded and tapped the plugs for rod ends.

During freshman-year integration, a missed tolerance stackup caused the apex to interfere at maximum steer. We checked the required material removal in Ansys and ground the existing apex to recover clearance. The combined suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb.

projects.headline: Pushrods & Control Arms
projects.unit: less suspension mass than the prior design
projects.challenge: At integration, the control-arm apex interfered before the car reached maximum steer. A tolerance stackup we had missed in the design caused the clearance problem.
projects.decision: Model the exact material removal needed at the apex, check the revised geometry in Ansys, then use an angle grinder to remove that material from the existing part.
projects.proof: The revised apex made maximum steer possible. The original suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb through the apex-mounted gussets and carbon-fiber pushrods.
projects.takeaway: That experience taught me how much engineering is working through the problem in front of you, one constraint at a time.

projects.title: Discrete Ride Height Adjustment
projects.summary: I designed a shim-based attachment to make ride-height changes more repeatable, replacing a process that relied on turning an opposite-thread pushrod.

points.text: The mechanism changes pushrod length by adding or removing shims and retightening the fasteners. The attachment connects to the inboard suspension mechanism and keeps the shim stack in compression.
I designed the attachment in 7075 aluminum and kept the shim pockets concentric with the retaining bolts. Lightweight shim geometry reduced the mass added by the adjustment mechanism.

I checked the attachment under pushrod loading in SolidWorks FEA. The shims were laser-cut and the attachment pieces machined; another team member CNC-machined the upper component. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car in exchange for repeatable adjustment.

projects.headline: Discrete Ride-Height Adjustment
projects.unit: added to the entire car for adjustability
projects.challenge: Make trackside ride-height changes more repeatable and easier to perform.
projects.decision: Use a 7075 aluminum attachment with removable shims for repeatable ride-height adjustment.
projects.proof: SolidWorks FEA checked the attachment under pushrod loading. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car.
projects.takeaway: A small weight penalty bought a more repeatable adjustment for the team at the track.

steps.text: I checked the attachment under pushrod loading in SolidWorks FEA. The shims were laser-cut and the attachment pieces machined; another team member CNC-machined the upper component. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car in exchange for repeatable adjustment.

code.name: PolicyMarket
code.desc: Address-driven civic app for exploring 2026 election candidates in your exact federal, state, and local districts. Resolves an address to coordinates and districts, discovers the races for that voter, and renders them on an interactive map with district overlays.
code.shotCap: State-level races for a resolved address, with the HD-15 boundary overlaid, candidates in the panel.

code.name: march-madness
code.desc: Monte Carlo simulation for my 2026 NCAA bracket. Models team strength, stylistic matchup clashes, and injury effects, weighted against a historical upset dataset.
code.shotCap: Full bracket from a 10,000-run simulation, with per-matchup advance probabilities.

code.name: Runtime-Terror
code.desc: Hackathon project visualising global geothermal hotspots on an interactive globe, built on the IHFC 2024 Global Heat Flow Database. With Amol Mathur, Jared Sturisky, and Arkady Marchenko.
code.shotCap: Heat-flow density over North America with the top-ranked geothermal sites called out.
